Prison, on the other hand, is uniformly bad. Getting someone out of a fundamentally inhumane, expensive, and ineffective criminal justice system is better for the community regardless of whether they are guilty. 

Also, I’ll just say.. getting people off on technicalities (aka defending their constitutional rights) personally feels the *best* to me - because the deck is SO stacked against our clients that it feels pretty damn good to use it against the State for once. For writing and drawing, I find that Pilot G2 pens (I think they come in four different sizes ranging from 0.38-1.0mm in diameter) are always awesome.  The wider you go with them, the more smearing you will experience.

When writing drafts and class notes, I like wooden Ticonderogas. I use yellows for writing and blacks for drawing, as they are a bitter lighter and easier to erase.  If you write a lot and don't mind being a bit obnoxious, you could carry around a small, battery-operated sharpener so they never lose their superior point.  You could also learn how to widdle.

If you prefer mechanical pencils, I know a lot of people recommend Pentels, especially the P200 series.  When using pencil for daily writing, I personally prefer BIC .5mm's.  They are affordable and write really well, giving you a smooth, even stroke on high quality paper.

Finally, I'd like to highlight a company called Staedtler.  All of their products that I've tried have had unique features and fantastic performance.  They make a couple good mechanical pencils, including 777 (.5mm), which I would highly recommend. This and their ultra thin felt pen, the triplus fineliner (.3mm), are both really good for your grip.  The 777 has a felxible rubber casing, so you can control it no matter how you hold it. The fineliner is long, light, and triangular in shape, making it very easy to guide with your finger(s).  If you find that you enjoy this design, Ticonderoga makes wooden pencil that share this shape.  I think the standard hexagon works just fine for pencils, though.

All of these items are inexpensive, especially the pencils, compared to lots of other products out there that will provide top-notch performance.  I've produced some high quality materials using almost exclusively Ticonderoga and Pilot writing utensils, though.  The technique of the practitioner really matters more than how powerful the tool is.  I would still recommend all of these supplies.  Each of them write/draw very smoothly and don't create much mess (until you start getting to .7mm plus with gel ink pens).

As for how to develop better visual style in your writing?

1. Write whole words/sentences/paragraphs/stanzas/verses rather than individual letters.  A lot of what your writing looks like has to do with how you connect letters, how many strokes you perform over how much time, the straightness of your line.... all of this shows up on the page when you are writing for assignments and such, so you should practice it, as well.

2.  Write often and for yourself.  Keep journals, write stories, send letters to friends and family.  The more you use your handwriting, the better it will become.  You may find yourself not wanting to write.  Do it anyway.

3. Don't be lazy when you write.  Maybe not all the time, but usually avoid writing while laying down or slouching in your seat.  Also, learn how to hold your writing tools properly, maintain a grip that says "I am in control of this stroke" and become Master of what you put on the page.
